I shudder in my soul when I think of how horribly helpless it must be to drown. Fighting the inbuilt need to breathe whilst consciously knowing that of you do it will kill you. That poor fucking person! :-(

As a swimmer who almost drowned in ~4 ft. of water - it's not that scary when you're trained. I used to do a down-and-back under water (50m) at the end of my workout, and one day I had either worked out particularly hard, or hadn't rested enough beforehand. On my way back I was holding back the struggle for air, and about 3-5 feet before I touched the side, everything kinda shrank down to tunnel vision starting to go black like it does when you're about to pass out. Then my hands touched the side, and I kicked up and took a breath. Then held onto the side a bit while the black faded, and I realized I almost drowned. It's really not nearly as scary as I'd imagined it would be; although it did give me a little existential crisis since I was alone in the pool room and probably would've died. What a shitty way to go right?

Now I suppose if I hadn't trained or if someone was holding me under then yes, it'd be different. But for a trained person like herself I imagine she just tried her best to swim to resurface, ignoring the urge to breath like she always does, then everything went black like it almost did for me.

Coding Horror's most recent article argues that we are unlikely to see VR mainstream in the next 5 years due to the technical challenges. He argues that helmets are too bulky and that the resolution looks worse than normal screens. What do you think?
Do you think VR is likely to become mainstream in the next 5 years?

I agree. Voice recognition is only usable very recently, after years and years of development and promises that it was the next big thing. It takes a great deal of work to make these technologies work. I don't think VR will take off until we have a better delivery system than bulky helmets and the like. I'd argue we might not see it become mainstream until we have cybernetic implants in our heads.

I'll decline on getting a chip implanted in my head, of course, as I don't want bloatware dreams about the McRib, available for a limited time only. Wake up and order a delicious McRib!

This comment was brought to you by McDonalds. When you crave delicious fast food, there's nothing virtual about the taste of the McRib!
Voice recognition still hasn't met most of its promise. We've still got such a long way to go.

Within 5 years it will be a healthy market, but not mainstream. The current generation of VR needs a decent gaming PC, and that's arguably not mainstream. On top of that you need an expensive VR headset. There are few games out there, almost all of them small indie titles. Some big games support VR, but what we need is games built for VR.

If the Oculus Rift would cost $100, would work with PC, PS4 and XBox One, and would have half a dozend AAA games build for VR it would be mainstream within two years despite all it's current limitations. With the stuff we are getting now, VR is closer to 10 years away from mainstream.
Nope. It's always been a gimmick and always will be.

I agree. People don't want to wear stuff on their face for entertainment. 3D tvs are out and how many people use those? Maybe a novelty at first, but I'll bet very few people use their 3D glasses after a few months.

I expect VR will become huge but it's not going to supplant existing game control schema.

Everything I've read makes it sound like playing current style FPS's on OR just doesn't work and I don't see it being a viable control system for strategy games.

Honestly more than anything I'm looking forward to exploring google street view with it and I heard Mythbusters is already filming with VR in mind.

Take a look at Elite Dangerous. I've played the demo on VR, and it was mindblowing.

Dogfighting in an asteroid field and the target heads up out of field of view? Just raise your head and look over your shoulder to keep him in sight while you pull up to follow. Quick glance down to ensure you're not going to hit anything, then back up to keep him in sight.

I also had a chance to play Asetto Corsa as well, with a force feedback wheel, pedals, and shifter. Corner coming up? Turn your head to the side to look at the track that's coming up. It's just so intuitive and immersive compared to a controller and a screen.

If the internet is any guide, PC gamers like to upgrade their tech on a regular basis. I see VR capabilities and a headset being one of those upgrades that just happens as a natural progression in technology. This Christmas is when the consumer sets are supposed to come out. Once your buddy gets a VR headset and you try it, you'll want one too.

I've worked with somebody working on VR applications for realtors, scanning houses inside and out, rebuilding them in VR, then shipping them cross-country for service members who are relocating. In our country, it's likely that a family only gets one day to house shop through everything before making a decision - the virtual walkthroughs allow a more detailed review of properties before flying out. Additionally, the same person is working on commercial realty applications, allowing virtual walkthroughs and buildouts before purchasing a commercial property.

I'm working on building out a VR development lab now, so that in 5 years when it's big, we'll be ready.

But I may be a bit biased on the subject.
